per_question.question: What are the general eligibility criteria for CAP/DA services under NC Medicaid?
per_question.agent_answer:
## General CAP/DA eligibility criteria

CAP/DA is a Home- and Community-Based Services waiver for adults with disabilities who are at risk of institutionalization. The person must be **age 18 or older** and meet NC Medicaid’s **long-term-care Medicaid eligibility** requirements to receive waiver services.

In general, the person must:

- Be enrolled in NC Medicaid and have an eligibility category that permits the CAP/DA service.
- Need a service that is medically necessary, individualized to the person’s diagnosis/symptoms and needs, safely deliverable, and not primarily for the convenience of the beneficiary, caregiver, or provider. The service also cannot have an equally effective, more conservative, or less costly statewide alternative.
- Meet the required HCBS nursing-facility level of care, as determined by NC Medicaid, and need long-term-care supports of the type usually provided in an institution because of documented medical and functional needs. The policy states that this is assessed quarterly.
- Have a CAP assessment showing a reasonable indication that they will need at least one CAP/DA waiver service within 30 calendar days of the evaluation.
- Have a signed service plan authorizing one or more waiver services monthly to help avoid institutionalization through coordinated case management—or, for a short-term equipment, modification, or technology need, have a signed plan designed to help the person return to or remain in their primary private residence and avoid institutional placement.
- Be able to maintain health, safety, and well-being at a primary private residence or other approved location with formal and informal supports.
- Have paid-care needs that can be met within the waiver’s average institutional-cost limit.
- Have a primary physician able to link and coordinate medical services.
- Have an emergency back-up and disaster plan identifying who will provide needed care if regular direct-care staff or the primary caregiver cannot do so, including during a public-health emergency. The plan must be completed during service-plan development or within 30 calendar days of initial or annual approval, and updated quarterly or during an emergency or pandemic.

The current policy is effective September 1, 2025; its all-sections revision reflects CMS approval of the CAP/DA waiver renewal effective November 1, 2024.

Medicaid shall cover procedures, products, and services related to this policy when they are medically necessary, and:
the procedure, product, or service is individualized, specific, and consistent with symptoms or confirmed diagnosis of the illness or injury under treatment, and not in excess of the beneficiary's needs;
the procedure, product, or service can be safely furnished, and no equally effective and more conservative or less costly treatment is available statewide; and
the procedure, product, or service is furnished in a manner not primarily intended for the convenience of the beneficiary, the beneficiary's caretaker, or the provider.

ID: sec:doc:clinical_policy:3K-2:3.2.1
Title: 3.2.1 Specific criteria covered by Medicaid
Section: 3.2.1
Policy: 3K-2
Type: clinical_policy
Citation link: [Community Alternatives Program for Disabled Adults (CAP/DA)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment)
Reason: General eligibility or coverage section from the preferred document.
Content:
Medicaid shall cover CAP/DA when the beneficiary meets the following specific criteria:
Meets the required HCBS nursing facility LOC as determined by NC Medicaid and requires long-term care support at a level typically provided in an institution that is directly related to a documented medical diagnosis and functional care need, as assessed quarterly;
The completed CAP assessment finds there is a reasonable indication that the individual would need a service plan for at least one of the CAP/DA HCBS within 30 calendar days of the evaluation. Refer to Appendix F for reasonable indication of need ;
Have a signed service plan that authorizes one or more waiver services to be rendered on a monthly basis, that mitigates institutionalization through coordinated case management;
Have a signed service plan that authorizes an installation of equipment, modification or technology, on a short-term basis, to return to or remain in the primary private residence to prevent an institutional placement (the installation of equipment or modification must be completed within three calendar months of service plan approval);
Able to maintain health, safety and well-being at their primary private residence or an approved location with the use of both formal and informal supports, refer to Appendix F for definition of informal supports;
Paid care needs can be maintained within the average institutional cost of the CAP/DA waiver;
Has a primary physician that can link and coordinate all medical services;
Has an emergency back-up and disaster plan that specifies who shall provide care when key direct care staff cannot provide services or tasks as indicated in the current plan of care (POC), when the primary caregiver is experiencing an emergency, and when there is a public health emergency such as a weather event or pandemic.
Note: An emergency and disaster plan is a mandatory requirement that must be completed during the service plan development or within 30 calendar days of the initial and annual CAP/DA service plan approval. The emergency and disaster plan must be updated quarterly or during an emergency or pandemic.
Medicaid shall cover Consumer-Directed services when a beneficiary meets all of the above and the following criteria:
Understands the rights and responsibilities of directing their own care as evidenced by the completion of a mandatory self-assessment questionnaire and successful completion of an introductory consumer direction training and orientation Refer to Appendix C ;
Willing and emotionally capable to assume the responsibilities of an employer under the consumer-directed care by ensuring health and safety and identifying training opportunities to build competencies for him or herself and hired personal assistants as evidenced by a completed mandatory self-assessment questionnaire, or selects a representative who is willing and capable to assume the responsibilities to direct the beneficiary's care; and
Meets the specific criteria listed in Subsection 3.2.2(a) (b), and the following requirements:
Must have an approved service plan that identifies the amount, duration, frequency, and national provider identifier (NPI) of CAP/DA services and non-CAP/DA services as indicated in the beneficiary's service plan and approved by the Case Management Entity (CME);
Must have services provided according to all requirements specified in this policy; all applicable federal and state laws, rules, and regulations; the current standards of practice; and provider agency policies and procedures; and
Must sign and adhere to Beneficiary Rights and Responsibilities to indicate willingness to participate in CAP/DA.

Section: 1.0

Citation link: [Community Alternatives Program for Disabled Adults (CAP/DA)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment)
Reason: Program scope or description section from the preferred document.
Content:
The Community Alternatives Program for Disabled Adults (CAP/DA) is a Medicaid Home and Community-Based Services (HCBS) Waiver authorized under section1915(c) of the Social Security Act and complies with 42 CFR § 440.180, Home and community-based waiver services. This waiver program provides a cost-effective alternative to institutionalization for a beneficiary, in a specified target population, who is at risk for institutionalization if specialized waiver services were not available. These services allow this targeted individual to remain in or return to a home and community-based setting.
HCBS waivers are approved by Centers of Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) for a specified time. The waiver establishes the requirements for program administration and funding. Federal regulations for HCBS waivers are found in 42 CFR Part 441 Subpart G, Home and Community-Based Services: Waiver Requirements. NC Medicaid can renew or amend the waiver with the approval of CMS. CMS may exercise its authority to terminate the waiver when it believes the waiver is not operated properly. The CAP/DA HCBS (referred to as CAP/DA for the purpose of this policy) is a waiver that serves an adult with disabilities 18 years of age and older who is at risk of institutionalization. To receive services from this waiver program as listed on the service plan, the individual shall meet the Medicaid eligibility requirements for long-term care.
Pursuant to 42 CFR§ 431.10, NC Medicaid is the administrative authority of the waiver and outlines the policies and procedures governing the waiver. NC Medicaid appoints local entities to provide the day-to-day operation of the waiver to ensure the primary six waiver assurances are met.

per_question.question: What DME items are specifically NOT covered by NC Medicaid under the Orthotics and Prosthetics policy, and what general criteria must be met for coverage?
per_question.agent_answer:
## Items specifically not covered

Under the Orthotics & Prosthetics policy, NC Medicaid does **not** cover:

- Devices intended for the beneficiary’s or caregiver’s comfort or convenience.  
- Backup devices or duplicates kept at different locations.  
- Devices and supplies for nursing-facility residents.  
- Devices or supplies another agency covers.  
- Equipment or supplies for a beneficiary receiving hospice care. [Policy 5B § 4.2.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/5b-orthotics-prosthetics/download?attachment)

The policy also excludes an orthotic or prosthetic procedure, product, or service if the beneficiary does not meet applicable eligibility or coverage criteria, if it duplicates another provider’s item or service, or if it is experimental, investigational, or part of a clinical trial. [Policy 5B § 4.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/5b-orthotics-prosthetics/download?attachment)

## General coverage criteria

Coverage requires all of the following:

- An order from a physician, physician assistant, or nurse practitioner.  
- Medical necessity to maintain or improve the beneficiary’s medical, physical, or functional level, with suitability for noninstitutional settings where normal life activities occur.  
- A documented face-to-face encounter with the ordering clinician related to the primary reason for the device within six months before orthotics or prosthetics begin.  
- Review of the beneficiary’s need by the ordering clinician at least annually. [Policy 5B § 3.2.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/5b-orthotics-prosthetics/download?attachment)

For an **orthotic**, medical necessity means it is needed to correct or prevent skeletal deformity, support or align movable body parts, or preserve or improve physical function. For a **prosthetic**, it must replace all or part of the function of a permanently inoperative, absent, or malfunctioning body part and be needed for mobility, daily care, or rehabilitation. [Policy 5B § 3.2.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/5b-orthotics-prosthetics/download?attachment)

The device must also be a reasonable and medically necessary part of the treatment plan, fit the beneficiary’s diagnosis, condition, functional limits, and symptoms, and be high quality with obtainable replacement parts. [Policy 5B § 3.2.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/5b-orthotics-prosthetics/download?attachment)

The policy’s additional-specific-exclusions subsection states that no further exclusions apply beyond those listed. [Policy 5B § 4.2.2](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/5b-orthotics-prosthetics/download?attachment)

All claims are supported by the evidence blocks. Citations are precise and section-level (§3.2.1, §4.1, §4.2.1, §4.2.2). The answer is comprehensive and well-organized, covering both the not-covered items and the general coverage criteria as asked. No hallucinations detected.

per_question.question: What are the entrance, continued service, and discharge criteria for outpatient behavioral health services in NC Medicaid?
per_question.agent_answer:
## NC Medicaid outpatient behavioral-health criteria

For outpatient behavioral health services, the beneficiary must meet the policy’s general medical-necessity standards: the service must be individualized and consistent with symptoms or diagnosis, safely furnished, not exceed need, have no equally effective more conservative or lower-cost statewide alternative, and not be primarily for convenience. [Policy 8C § 3.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8c-outpatient-behavioral-health-services-provided-direct-enrolled-providers/download?attachment) Policy 8C does not require prior approval for these services. [Policy 8C § 5.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8c-outpatient-behavioral-health-services-provided-direct-enrolled-providers/download?attachment)

### Entrance (admission) criteria — **all must be met**
1. The beneficiary has a current DSM-5 diagnosis (or diagnosis under a subsequent edition of that reference).  
2. The beneficiary has behavioral, psychological, or biological dysfunction and functional impairment consistent with and associated with that diagnosis.  
3. If a higher level of care is indicated but unavailable, or the beneficiary refuses it, outpatient treatment may be used until the appropriate level is available or to help the beneficiary participate in that higher level of care.  
4. The beneficiary can develop skills to manage symptoms, make behavioral changes, and respond favorably to therapeutic interventions.  
5. There is no evidence that alternative interventions would be more effective under NC community-practice standards. [Policy 8C § 3.2.1.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8c-outpatient-behavioral-health-services-provided-direct-enrolled-providers/download?attachment)

### Continued-service criteria — **one from each group must be met**
**First, at least one of these must apply:**
- The desired outcome or level of functioning has not been restored, improved, or sustained within the treatment-plan timeframe;
- The beneficiary remains at risk of relapse based on the current clinical assessment and history; **or**
- The functional gains are tenuous.

**And, in addition, at least one of these must apply:**
- The beneficiary has achieved current treatment-plan goals, but documented symptoms show that additional goals are indicated; **or**
- The beneficiary is making satisfactory progress toward goals, and documentation supports that continuing the service is expected to effectively address the treatment-plan goals. [Policy 8C § 3.2.1.2](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8c-outpatient-behavioral-health-services-provided-direct-enrolled-providers/download?attachment)

### Discharge criteria — **any one is sufficient**
- The beneficiary’s functioning has improved in relation to the treatment-plan goals;
- The beneficiary or legally responsible person no longer wants the services; **or**
- Despite treatment-plan modifications, the beneficiary has not improved and needs a more appropriate best-practice or evidence-based treatment modality under NC community-practice standards. [Policy 8C § 3.2.1.3](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8c-outpatient-behavioral-health-services-provided-direct-enrolled-providers/download?attachment)

The current policy is effective April 15, 2025; its most recent amendment corrected telephonic-service language and removed a prior-authorization requirement for telephone-only services. [Policy 8C Change Notice 2025-04-15](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8c-outpatient-behavioral-health-services-provided-direct-enrolled-providers/download?attachment)

ID: sec:doc:clinical_policy:8C:3.2.1.1

Content:
All of the following criteria are necessary for admission of a beneficiary to outpatient treatment services:
A current Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition [(DSM-5) or any subsequent editions of this reference material] diagnosis;
The beneficiary presents behavioral, psychological, or biological dysfunction and functional impairment, which are consistent and associated with the current diagnosis;
If a higher level of care is indicated but unavailable or the beneficiary is refusing the service, outpatient services can be provided until the appropriate level of care is available or to support the beneficiary to participate in that higher level of care;
The beneficiary is capable of developing skills to manage symptoms, make behavioral changes, and respond favorably to therapeutic interventions;
There is no evidence to support that alternative interventions would be more effective, based on North Carolina community practice standards (Best Practice Guidelines of the American Academy of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry, American Psychiatric Association, American Board of Addiction Medicine)

per_question.question: How does the EPSDT special provision affect coverage for outpatient therapy services, and what ordering practitioner requirements apply to beneficiaries under 21?
per_question.agent_answer:
## EPSDT effect on outpatient therapy coverage

For a Medicaid beneficiary under 21, EPSDT can allow outpatient specialized-therapy limits—such as limits on scope, amount, duration, frequency, location, or other policy criteria—to be exceeded or not applied when the provider documents that the therapy is medically necessary to correct or ameliorate the child’s identified condition.

The documentation must show how the service will improve or maintain health, compensate for the problem, prevent worsening, or prevent additional health problems.

EPSDT does not require coverage of care that is unsafe, ineffective, experimental/investigational, nonmedical, or not generally accepted medical practice.

This is not an automatic entitlement to a particular therapy or quantity of therapy: the service must still be medically necessary, and outpatient specialized therapies generally require prior approval before treatment.

Being under 21 does not waive the prior-approval requirement.

For beneficiaries under 21, the prior-approval request must include information demonstrating that all EPSDT criteria are met and, when available, supporting evidence-based literature.

## Ordering practitioner requirement

The outpatient specialized-therapy service must be ordered by an NC Medicaid-enrolled MD, DO, DPM, certified nurse midwife, physician assistant, or nurse practitioner.

Separately, the therapy treatment plan must be established after an evaluation and before treatment begins, developed with the medical provider and—with respect to children—the beneficiary’s parent(s) or legal guardian(s). It must include, among other items, the therapy diagnosis, measurable goals, interventions, frequency, visit length, plan dates, and the completing professional’s name, credentials, and signature.

Policy 10A is current in the retrieved materials with an effective date of February 1, 2025.

Section: 3.2.1.3
Policy: 10A

Reason: EPSDT or pediatric service section from the preferred document.
Content:
Medicaid shall cover medically necessary outpatient speech-language therapy treatment for a beneficiary when prior authorization is received. Refer to Section 5.0.
Medically necessary treatment for oral phase, pharyngeal phase, or oropharyngeal phase dysphagia must contain documented findings.
These findings must address ONE of the following deficits consistent with a dysphagia diagnosis:
Coughing and choking while eating or drinking;
Coughing, choking or drooling with swallowing;
Wet-sounding voice;
Changes in breathing when eating or drinking;
Frequent respiratory infections;
Known or suspected aspiration pneumonia;
Masses on the tongue, pharynx or larynx;
Muscle weakness, or myopathy, involving the pharynx;
Neuromuscular degenerative disease likely to affect swallowing regardless of the presence of a communication difficulty;
Medical issues that affect feeding, swallowing, and nutrition; or
Oral function impairment or deficit that interferes with feeding.
These findings must be indicated through ONE of the following:
Video fluoroscopic swallowing exam (VFSE), also sometimes called a modified barium swallow exam (MBS);
Fiber optic endoscopic evaluation of swallowing (FEES); or,
Clinical feeding and swallowing evaluation.
For a beneficiary who is a minority language speaker, there is a continuum of proficiency in English.
Determination of the minority language speaker's proficiency on the continuum must be documented as one of the following:
Bilingual English proficient: a beneficiary who is bilingual and who is fluent in English or has greater control of English than the minority language;
Limited English proficient: a bilingual or monolingual beneficiary who is proficient in his or her native language, but not English; or
Limited in both English and the minority language : a beneficiary who is limited in both English and the minority language exhibits limited communication competence in both languages.
Evaluation must contain both objective and subjective measures to determine if the beneficiary is more proficient in either the English language or the minority language.
For speech and language therapy services to be medically necessary for a beneficiary who is a minority language speaker, ALL the following criteria must be met:
All speech deficits must be present in the language in which the beneficiary has the highest proficiency;
All language deficits must be present in the language in which the beneficiary has the highest proficiency;
The delivery of services must be in the language in which the beneficiary has the highest receptive language proficiency; and
If the use of interpreters or translators is the only alternative, the speech-language pathologist or audiologist must:
Provide sufficient instruction to the interpreter or translator regarding the purposes, procedures and goals of the tests and therapy methods;
For each date of service, the provider must ensure the interpreter or translator understands his or her role as it relates to the clinical procedures to be used and responses expected to address the goal;
Use the same interpreter or translator with a given beneficiary as consistently as possible; and
Use observation or other nonlinguistic measures as supplements to the translated measures, such as (1) beneficiary's interaction with parents, (2) beneficiary's interaction with peers, (3) pragmatic analysis.

ID: sec:doc:clinical_policy:10A:2.2.1
Title: 2.2.1 EPSDT Special Provision: Exception to Policy Limitations for a Medicaid Beneficiary under 21 Years of Age
Section: 2.2.1
Policy: 10A
Type: clinical_policy
Citation link: [Clinical Coverage Policy 10A](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment)
Reason: EPSDT or pediatric service section from the preferred document.
Content:
42 U.S.C. § 1396d(r) [1905(r) of the Social Security Act]
Early and Periodic Screening, Diagnostic, and Treatment (EPSDT) is a federal Medicaid requirement that requires the state Medicaid agency to cover services, products, or procedures for Medicaid beneficiary under 21 years of age if the service is medically necessary health care to correct or ameliorate a defect, physical or mental illness, or a condition [health problem] identified through a screening examination ** (includes any evaluation by a physician or other licensed clinician).
This means EPSDT covers most of the medical or remedial care a child needs to improve or maintain his or her health in the best condition possible, compensate for a health problem, prevent it from worsening, or prevent the development of additional health problems.
Medically necessary services will be provided in the most economic mode, as long as the treatment made available is similarly efficacious to the service requested by the beneficiary's physician, therapist, or other licensed practitioner; the determination process does not delay the delivery of the needed service; and the determination does not limit the beneficiary's right to a free choice of providers.
EPSDT does not require the state Medicaid agency to provide any service, product or procedure:
that is unsafe, ineffective, or experimental or investigational.
that is not medical in nature or not generally recognized as an accepted method of medical practice or treatment.
Service limitations on scope, amount, duration, frequency, location of service, and other specific criteria described in clinical coverage policies may be exceeded or may not apply as long as the provider's documentation shows that the requested service is medically necessary 'to correct or ameliorate a defect, physical or mental illness, or a condition' [health problem]; that is, provider documentation shows how the service, product, or procedure meets all EPSDT criteria, including to correct or improve or maintain the beneficiary's health in the best condition possible, compensate for a health problem, prevent it from worsening, or prevent the development of additional health problems.

ID: sec:doc:clinical_policy:10A:3.2.1.4
Title: 3.2.1.4 Audiology Therapy (Aural Rehabilitation)
Section: 3.2.1.4
Policy: 10A
Type: clinical_policy
Citation link: [Clinical Coverage Policy 10A](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment)
Reason: EPSDT or pediatric service section from the preferred document.
Content:
Medicaid shall cover medically necessary audiology services when the beneficiary demonstrates the following:
the presence of any degree or type of hearing loss on the basis of the results of an audiologic (aural) rehabilitation evaluation; or
the presence of impaired or compromised auditory processing abilities based on the results of a central auditory test battery.
A beneficiary shall have one or more of the following deficits to initiate therapy:
hearing loss (any type) with a pure tone average greater than 25dB in either ear;
Standard Score more than one SD (standard deviation) below normal for chronological age on standardized tests of language, audition, speech, or auditory processing which must be documented on the basis of the results of a central auditory test battery; or
less than 1-year gain in skills (auditory, speech, processing) during a period of 12-calendar months.
Aural rehabilitation consists of:
facilitating receptive and expressive communication of a beneficiary with hearing loss;
achieving improved, augmented or compensated communication processes;
improving auditory processing, listening, spoken language processing, auditory memory, overall communication process; and
benefiting learning and daily activities.
Evaluation for aural rehabilitation
Service delivery requires ALL the following elements:
The provider shall check the functioning of hearing aids, assistive listening systems and devices, and sensory aids prior to the evaluation.
Through interview, observation, and clinical testing, the provider shall evaluate the beneficiary's skills, in both clinical and natural environments, for the following:
medical and audiological history;
reception, comprehension, and production of language in oral, or manual language modalities;
speech and voice production;
perception of speech and non-speech stimuli in multiple modalities;
listening skills;
speech-reading; and
communication strategies.
The provider shall determine the specific functional limitation(s), which must be measurable, for the beneficiary.
Evaluation for Central Auditory Processing Disorders (CAPD)
CAPD evaluation is to be completed by an audiologist and consists of tests to evaluate the beneficiary's overall auditory function. Through interview, observation, and clinical testing, the provider shall evaluate the beneficiary for ALL the following:
Communication, medical, and educational history;
Medicaid shall cover the following Central auditory tests for the identification of CAPD:
auditory discrimination test;
auditory temporal processing and patterning test;
 dichotic speech test;
 monaural low-redundancy speech test;
binaural interaction test;
 electroacoustic measures; and
electrophysiologic measures.
Interpretation of evaluations are derived from the beneficiary's performance on multiple tests. The diagnosis of CAPD must be based on a score of two standard deviations below the mean on at least two central auditory tests.
The provider shall determine the specific functional limitation(s), which must be measurable, for the beneficiary.
Functional deficits consist of  a beneficiary's inability to:
hear normal conversational speech;
hear conversation via the telephone;
identify, by hearing, environmental sounds necessary for safety (such as siren, car horn, doorbell, baby crying);
understand conversational speech (in person or via telephone);
hear and understand teacher in classroom setting;
hear and understand classmates during class discussion;
hear and understand co-workers or supervisors during meetings at work;
hear and process the super-segmental aspects of speech or the phonemes of speech; or
localize sound.
Language therapy treatment sessions must not be billed concurrently with aural rehabilitation therapy treatment sessions.
Note : This policy does not address postoperative diagnostic analysis and programming of cochlear and auditory brainstem implant services performed by licensed audiologists. For coverage criteria for these services, refer to Clinical Coverage Policy 1A-4, Cochlear and Auditory Brainstem Implants , found on NC Medicaid's website https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/

Content:
Prior approval is required prior to the start of all treatment services. For a Local Education Agency (LEA), the prior approval process is deemed met by the IEP, IFSP, IHP, BIP or 504 Plan processes.
Detailed information and instructions for registering and submitting requests is available on the DHHS utilization review contractor's website https://choicepa.medicaidprograms.org/Account/Login.aspx?ReturnUrl=%2f
The provider shall submit a request to DHHS utilization review contractor to start the approval process. Please note that approval, if granted, is for medical approval only and does not guarantee payment or ensure beneficiary eligibility on the date of service.
The provider shall submit information supporting that all EPSDT criteria are met and evidence-based literature supporting the request, if available.

per_question.question: Does NC Medicaid cover Personal Care Services for beneficiaries who live in an assisted living facility?
per_question.agent_answer:
**Yes—NC Medicaid can cover Personal Care Services (PCS) for a beneficiary living in an assisted living facility, if the facility is a North Carolina–licensed Adult Care Home and the beneficiary meets the policy’s eligibility and service criteria.** PCS in congregate settings is delivered by paraprofessional aides employed by licensed home care agencies, licensed Adult Care Homes, or licensed supervised-living-home staff. [Policy 3L-1 § 1.0](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/media/14986/download?attachment)

Among other requirements, the beneficiary must have qualifying unmet needs for specified activities of daily living, reside in an eligible licensed congregate setting, have no other payer responsible for PCS, lack an available/willing/able informal caregiver for the authorized service periods, be under a physician’s ongoing direct care for the condition causing the functional limitations, and be medically stable without needing continuous licensed-nurse or other licensed-professional care or monitoring. [Policy 3L-1 § 3.2.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/media/14986/download?attachment)

Coverage is not available, for example, when the required independent assessment or authorization has not been completed, services exceed the approved amount or occur outside the authorized period, the service is provided somewhere other than the person’s primary congregate living setting, or an available informal caregiver can regularly meet the personal-care need. [Policy 3L-1 § 4.2.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/media/14986/download?attachment)

It correctly identifies that NC Medicaid covers PCS in congregate settings under Policy 3L-1, specifies that the facility must be a licensed Adult Care Home, accurately summarizes the eligibility criteria from Section 3.2.1 (ADL requirements, physician care, medical stability, no informal caregiver, no third-party payer), and correctly notes non-coverage conditions from Section 4.2.1. All claims are supported by the evidence blocks. The answer cites specific policy sections (§ 1.0, § 3.2.1, § 4.2.1) with links. The answer aligns well with the reference answer's key points about Policy 3L-1 governing congregate settings, Section 3.2.1 criteria, and non-covered services. No hallucinations detected.

Section: 3.2.1

Reason: Additional scope or not-covered section for the yes/no coverage question.
Content:
Medicaid shall cover State Plan Personal Care Services (PCS) Provided in Congregate Settings when the beneficiary meets the following specific criteria and other items in this section:
has a medical or mental condition, disability, or cognitive impairment and demonstrates unmet needs for, at a minimum:
three of the five qualifying activities of daily living (ADLs) with limited hands-on assistance. Refer to Subsection 5.4.3;
two ADLs, one of which requires extensive assistance; or
two ADLs, one of which requires assistance at the full dependence level.
resides in:
a congregate facility licensed by the State of North Carolina as an Adult Care Home (ACH) as defined in NC G.S. §131D-2.1, a combination home as defined in NC G.S. § 131E-101; or
a group home licensed under Chapter 122C of the General Statutes and under 10A NCAC 27G .5601 (b)(2) as a supervised living facility for two or more adults whose primary diagnosis is mental illness, a developmental disability, or substance abuse dependency and is eligible to receive personal care services under the Medicaid State Plan.
In addition to the specific criteria in Subsection 3.2.1 a and b of this policy, the following criteria must be met:
The congregate setting is safe and free of health hazards for the beneficiary and PCS provider(s), as determined by a facility environmental assessment conducted by NC Medicaid or a DHHS designated contractor;
The congregate setting has received inspection conducted by the Division of Health Service Regulation (DHSR)
The place of service is safe for the beneficiary to receive PCS and for an aide to provide PCS;
No other third-party payer is responsible for covering PCS;
No family or household member or other informal caregiver is available, willing, and able to provide the authorized services during those periods of time when the services are provided;
The required PCS are directly linked to a documented medical or mental condition or physical or cognitive impairment causing the functional limitations requiring the PCS;
The beneficiary is under the ongoing direct care of a physician for the medical condition or diagnosis causing the functional limitations; and
The beneficiary is medically stable and does not require continuous care, monitoring (precautionary observation), or supervision (observation resulting in an intervention) by a licensed nurse or other licensed health care professional; and
Screening for Serious Mental Illness (SMI) in Adult Care Homes licensed under G.S. §131D-2.4 Effective November 1, 2018, any Medicaid beneficiary referred to or seeking admission to Adult Care Homes licensed under G.S. 131D-2.4 must be referred to a Tailored Plan Transition Coordinator for the Referral Screening Verification Process. Adult Care Home providers licensed under G.S. § 131D-2.4 shall not receive a PCS assessment or prior approval without verification of a Referral Screening ID.

### 4.2.1 Medicaid Additional Criteria Not Covered
Medicaid shall not cover Personal Care Services in Congregate Settings when:

a reassessment has not been completed within 30 calendar days of the end date of the previous prior authorization period because the beneficiary refused the assessment, could not be reached to schedule the assessment, or did not attend the scheduled assessment;

the PCS is provided at a location other than the beneficiary's primary congregate living setting;
the PCS exceeds the amount approved by the Comprehensive Independent Assessment Entity (CIAE);
the PCS is not completed on the date the service is billed;
the PCS is provided prior to the effective date or after the end date of the prior authorized service period;
the PCS is performed by an individual who is the beneficiary's legally responsible person, spouse, child, parent, sibling, grandparent, grandchild, or equivalent step or in-law relationship to the beneficiary;
Clinical Coverage Policy No: 3L-1
Amended Date:
family members or other informal caregivers are willing, able, and available on a regular basis adequate to meet the beneficiary's need for personal care; or
independent medical information does not validate the assessment, PCS hours may be reduced, denied, or terminated based on the additional information.
Note

Medicaid shall not cover PCS when rendered concurrently with another substantially equivalent Federal or State funded service. Services equivalent to PCS are:
home health aide services and in-home aide services in the Community Alternatives Programs (CAP/Choice, CAP/Disabled Adults); and
Private Duty Nursing (PDN).

per_question.question: Does NC Medicaid cover chiropractic services under Clinical Coverage Policy 5B?
per_question.agent_answer:
**No.** Clinical Coverage Policy 5B does not cover chiropractic services; it governs **orthotic and prosthetic devices**, not chiropractic treatment. It covers qualifying devices prescribed by the beneficiary’s treating physician, physician assistant, or nurse practitioner when medical necessity is documented. [Policy 5B § 1.0](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/5b-orthotics-prosthetics/download?attachment)

Under Policy 5B, Medicaid also does not cover a service governed by that policy if the beneficiary does not meet the policy’s eligibility or coverage criteria, if it duplicates another provider’s service, or if it is experimental, investigational, or part of a clinical trial. [Policy 5B § 4.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/5b-orthotics-prosthetics/download?attachment)

So Policy 5B cannot be used as authority for coverage of a chiropractic visit or spinal manipulation.

---

*Suggested citations for uncited claims above:*
- [Policy 5B § 4.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/5b-orthotics-prosthetics/download?attachment)

For beneficiaries under age 21, please request an 'EPSDT review' using NCTracks. Refer to section 2.2 Special Provisions for more information about EPSDT. ID: sec:doc:clinical_policy:5B:1.0
Title: 1.0 Description of the Procedure, Product, or Service
Section: 1.0
Policy: 5B
Type: clinical_policy
Citation link: [Orthotics & Prosthetics](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/5b-orthotics-prosthetics/download?attachment)

Content:
Orthotic and prosthetic devices are covered by NC Medicaid (Medicaid) when they are prescribed by the beneficiary's treating physician, physician's assistant, or nurse practitioner and medical necessity is documented. An orthotic or prosthetic device is medically necessary if it is needed to maintain or improve a beneficiary's medical, physical, or functional level.
Covered orthotic and prosthetic devices become the property of the beneficiary.
Refer to Attachment B for a list of HCPCS codes, established lifetime expectancies, quantity limitations, and required provider certification for Orthotics and Prosthetics.
For the rates associated with the list of HCPCS codes found in Attachment B, refer to the Orthotics and Prosthetics fee schedule at https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/providers.
In compliance with the CMS Home Health Final Rule Title 42, §440.70, items not listed in Attachment B or in the Orthotics and Prosthetics fee schedule may be considered for coverage if requested by a provider, or a beneficiary through a provider, and submitted for prior authorization (PA) review of medical necessity. For beneficiaries under age 21, please request an 'EPSDT review' using NCTracks. Refer to section 2.2 Special Provisions for more information about EPSDT. For beneficiaries aged 21 and older, please submit the request through NCTracks per the procedure detailed in Attachment E: Requesting Unlisted Orthotics and Prosthetics for Adults .

Primary sections:
ID: sec:doc:clinical_policy:10A:3.2.1.6
Title: 3.2.1.6 Treatment Plan (Plan of Care)
Section: 3.2.1.6
Policy: 10A
Type: clinical_policy
Citation link: [Clinical Coverage Policy 10A](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment)
Reason: Matched treatment.
Content:
The treatment plan must be established once an evaluation has been administered and prior to the beginning of treatment services. The treatment plan is developed in conjunction with the medical provider, beneficiary, parent(s) or legal guardian(s) for children, and Authorized Representative for adults (if applicable). The treatment plan must consider performance in both clinical and natural environments. Treatment must be culturally appropriate. Short- and long-term functional goals and specific objectives must be determined from the evaluation. Goals and objectives must be reviewed periodically and must target functional and measurable outcomes. The treatment plan must be a specific document.
Each treatment plan in combination with the evaluation or re-evaluation written report must contain ALL the following:
duration of the therapy treatment plan consisting of the start and end date (no more than six months);
discipline specific treatment diagnosis and any related medical diagnoses;
rehabilitative or habilitative potential;
defined goals (specific and measurable goals that have reasonable expectation to be achieved within the duration of the therapy plan) for each therapeutic discipline;
skilled interventions, methodology, procedures and specific programs to be utilized;
frequency of services;
length of each treatment visit in minutes; and
name, credentials and signature of professional completing the Treatment Plan dated on or prior to the start date of the treatment plan.

ID: sec:doc:clinical_policy:10A:_s36
Title: Treatment services must adhere to the following requirements:
Policy: 10A
Type: clinical_policy
Citation link: [Clinical Coverage Policy 10A](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment)
Reason: Matched documentation.
Content:
A verbal or a written order must be obtained for services prior to the start of services. All verbal orders must report the date and signature of the person receiving the order, must be recorded in the beneficiary's health record and shall be countersigned by the physician within 60 calendar days. All verbal orders are valid up to six months from the documented date of receipt . All written orders are valid up to six months from the date of the physician's signature. Backdating is not allowed.
All services must be provided according to a treatment plan that meets the requirements in Subsection 3.2.1.6.
Service providers shall review and renew or revise treatment plans and goals at least every six calendar months.
Prior approval is required prior to the start of treatment services.
For a Local Education Agency (LEA), the prior approval process is deemed met by the Individualized Education Program (IEP), Individual Family Service Plan (IFSP), Individual Health Plan (IHP), Behavior Intervention Plan (BIP), or 504 Plan processes. An LEA provider shall review, renew and revise the IEP, IFSP, IHP, BIP or 504 Plan annually along with obtaining a dated physician order with signature. The requirement of parent notification must occur at regular intervals throughout the year as stipulated by NC Department of Public Instruction. Such notification must detail how progress is sufficient to enable the child to achieve the goals by the end of the school year.
Faxed orders and faxed signatures are permissible and serve the same purposes for documentation as an original signature on an original form or order sheet. Electronic signatures and printed dates are acceptable. Providers using electronic signatures shall maintain policies regarding the use of electronic documentation addressing the security of records and the unique signature, sanctions against improper or unauthorized use, and reconstruction of records in the event of a system breakdown. Stamped signatures are not permitted.
Instructional training of the beneficiary, parent(s) or legal guardian(s) that incorporates activities and strategies to target the goals and facilitate progress must be considered when appropriate for the therapeutic place of service.

Supporting sections:
ID: sec:doc:clinical_policy:10A:3.2.1.4
Title: 3.2.1.4 Audiology Therapy (Aural Rehabilitation)
Section: 3.2.1.4
Policy: 10A
Type: clinical_policy
Citation link: [Clinical Coverage Policy 10A](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment)
Reason: Matched limitation.
Content:
Medicaid shall cover medically necessary audiology services when the beneficiary demonstrates the following:
the presence of any degree or type of hearing loss on the basis of the results of an audiologic (aural) rehabilitation evaluation; or
the presence of impaired or compromised auditory processing abilities based on the results of a central auditory test battery.
A beneficiary shall have one or more of the following deficits to initiate therapy:
hearing loss (any type) with a pure tone average greater than 25dB in either ear;
Standard Score more than one SD (standard deviation) below normal for chronological age on standardized tests of language, audition, speech, or auditory processing which must be documented on the basis of the results of a central auditory test battery; or
less than 1-year gain in skills (auditory, speech, processing) during a period of 12-calendar months.
Aural rehabilitation consists of:
facilitating receptive and expressive communication of a beneficiary with hearing loss;
achieving improved, augmented or compensated communication processes;
improving auditory processing, listening, spoken language processing, auditory memory, overall communication process; and
benefiting learning and daily activities.
Evaluation for aural rehabilitation
Service delivery requires ALL the following elements:
The provider shall check the functioning of hearing aids, assistive listening systems and devices, and sensory aids prior to the evaluation.
Through interview, observation, and clinical testing, the provider shall evaluate the beneficiary's skills, in both clinical and natural environments, for the following:
medical and audiological history;
reception, comprehension, and production of language in oral, or manual language modalities;
speech and voice production;
perception of speech and non-speech stimuli in multiple modalities;
listening skills;
speech-reading; and
communication strategies.
The provider shall determine the specific functional limitation(s), which must be measurable, for the beneficiary.
Evaluation for Central Auditory Processing Disorders (CAPD)
CAPD evaluation is to be completed by an audiologist and consists of tests to evaluate the beneficiary's overall auditory function. Through interview, observation, and clinical testing, the provider shall evaluate the beneficiary for ALL the following:
Communication, medical, and educational history;
Medicaid shall cover the following Central auditory tests for the identification of CAPD:
auditory discrimination test;
auditory temporal processing and patterning test;
 dichotic speech test;
 monaural low-redundancy speech test;
binaural interaction test;
 electroacoustic measures; and
electrophysiologic measures.
Interpretation of evaluations are derived from the beneficiary's performance on multiple tests. The diagnosis of CAPD must be based on a score of two standard deviations below the mean on at least two central auditory tests.
The provider shall determine the specific functional limitation(s), which must be measurable, for the beneficiary.
Functional deficits consist of  a beneficiary's inability to:
hear normal conversational speech;
hear conversation via the telephone;
identify, by hearing, environmental sounds necessary for safety (such as siren, car horn, doorbell, baby crying);
understand conversational speech (in person or via telephone);
hear and understand teacher in classroom setting;
hear and understand classmates during class discussion;
hear and understand co-workers or supervisors during meetings at work;
hear and process the super-segmental aspects of speech or the phonemes of speech; or
localize sound.
Language therapy treatment sessions must not be billed concurrently with aural rehabilitation therapy treatment sessions.
Note : This policy does not address postoperative diagnostic analysis and programming of cochlear and auditory brainstem implant services performed by licensed audiologists. For coverage criteria for these services, refer to Clinical Coverage Policy 1A-4, Cochlear and Auditory Brainstem Implants , found on NC Medicaid's website https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/

Content:
Medicaid shall require prior approval for Outpatient Specialized Therapies. The provider shall obtain prior approval before rendering Outpatient Specialized Therapies.
Note: Refer to Subsections 3.2.1.5, 5.1.2, and 5.2 for prior authorization exclusions.
To obtain prior approval, the request must clearly indicate that the service of a licensed therapist is required. Retroactive prior approval is considered when a beneficiary does not have Medicaid coverage at the time of the procedure and is later approved for Medicaid with a retroactive eligibility date. Medicaid does not guarantee approval of retroactive requests.

[getSection]
ID: sec:doc:clinical_policy:10A:_s36
Title: Treatment services must adhere to the following requirements:
Policy: 10A
Type: clinical_policy
Effective: 2025-02-01
Citation link: [Clinical Coverage Policy 10A](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment)

Content:
A verbal or a written order must be obtained for services prior to the start of services. All verbal orders must report the date and signature of the person receiving the order, must be recorded in the beneficiary's health record and shall be countersigned by the physician within 60 calendar days. All verbal orders are valid up to six months from the documented date of receipt . All written orders are valid up to six months from the date of the physician's signature. Backdating is not allowed.
All services must be provided according to a treatment plan that meets the requirements in Subsection 3.2.1.6.
Service providers shall review and renew or revise treatment plans and goals at least every six calendar months.
Prior approval is required prior to the start of treatment services.
For a Local Education Agency (LEA), the prior approval process is deemed met by the Individualized Education Program (IEP), Individual Family Service Plan (IFSP), Individual Health Plan (IHP), Behavior Intervention Plan (BIP), or 504 Plan processes. An LEA provider shall review, renew and revise the IEP, IFSP, IHP, BIP or 504 Plan annually along with obtaining a dated physician order with signature. The requirement of parent notification must occur at regular intervals throughout the year as stipulated by NC Department of Public Instruction. Such notification must detail how progress is sufficient to enable the child to achieve the goals by the end of the school year.
Faxed orders and faxed signatures are permissible and serve the same purposes for documentation as an original signature on an original form or order sheet. Electronic signatures and printed dates are acceptable. Providers using electronic signatures shall maintain policies regarding the use of electronic documentation addressing the security of records and the unique signature, sanctions against improper or unauthorized use, and reconstruction of records in the event of a system breakdown. Stamped signatures are not permitted.
Instructional training of the beneficiary, parent(s) or legal guardian(s) that incorporates activities and strategies to target the goals and facilitate progress must be considered when appropriate for the therapeutic place of service.

Content:
Medicaid shall require prior approval for Outpatient Specialized Therapies. The provider shall obtain prior approval before rendering Outpatient Specialized Therapies.
Note: Refer to Subsections 3.2.1.5, 5.1.2, and 5.2 for prior authorization exclusions.
To obtain prior approval, the request must clearly indicate that the service of a licensed therapist is required. Retroactive prior approval is considered when a beneficiary does not have Medicaid coverage at the time of the procedure and is later approved for Medicaid with a retroactive eligibility date. Medicaid does not guarantee approval of retroactive requests.

per_question.question: Can a CAP/DA beneficiary transfer between service providers, and what rules govern transfers of eligible beneficiaries?
per_question.agent_answer:
## Yes—CAP/DA beneficiaries may change service providers.

Under the current CAP/DA policy, a provider-agency change requires a [unverified: plan-of-care (POC) update], but it is not treated as a service-plan revision. The Case Management Entity (CME) must obtain a [unverified: Freedom of Choice of Provider form] signed by the beneficiary or responsible party consenting to the new provider.

That rule implements the broader provider-choice principle: an eligible Medicaid beneficiary may seek care from any willing and qualified service provider as defined under the State's Medicaid Plan, according to 42 CFR 431.51(a)(1).

## Transfers between counties or case-management entities

For a transfer to another county or entity, the CME must coordinate the transfer by the agreed transition date or within 30 calendar days after the request. The transfer process must prevent gaps in services and include: determining the anticipated service start date; coordinating a transition plan between provider agencies; planning for the beneficiary’s health, safety, and well-being; transferring the electronic health record through the CAP Business System; arranging a receiving-entity home visit within five business days after the move; and arranging for services to begin on the first transfer date.

For an active CAP/DA beneficiary moving counties, the transferring and receiving CME designees must coordinate on the agreed date or within 30 days; the receiving CME must conduct the post-move home visit and arrange services to begin on the transfer date.

An already-approved CAP/DA beneficiary may remain in CAP/DA after moving to another county; county residence does not end CAP/DA eligibility, although ongoing Medicaid eligibility is determined at the next Medicaid certification period. If the originating county has an active waitlist, the transferred beneficiary has priority status and is guaranteed a slot immediately in the receiving county.

## Provider qualifications and policy status

The selected provider still must be a qualified NC Medicaid CAP provider, approved through the required process, registered in the CAP Business System, and able to accept, decline, or acknowledge service authorizations within three business days.

The governing policy is Clinical Coverage Policy 3K-2, effective September 1, 2025. Its 2025 revision updated the policy to align with the CMS-approved CAP/DA waiver renewal effective November 1, 2024; the revision also made a minor wording change in § 3.3 concerning the birth month for CAP/C-to-CAP/DA transfers.

---

*Suggested citations for uncited claims above:*
- [Policy 3K-2 § 5.4.5](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment)
- [42 CFR § 431.51](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-431)
- [Policy 3K-2 § 3.3](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment)
- [Policy 3K-2 § 6.5](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment)
- [Policy 3K-2 Revision — 2025-09-01 (All sections and attachments)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment)

The answer correctly notes the POC update requirement for provider agency changes, the Freedom of Choice form requirement, the county transfer rules, priority status for transferring beneficiaries, and provider qualification requirements. The [unverified:] markers are appropriately used for claims the agent flagged as uncertain, which is honest disclosure rather than hallucination. The slight hallucination deduction is for the claim that '§ 3.3 concerning the birth month for CAP/C-to-CAP/DA transfers' was a minor wording change - the amendment evidence (doc:change_notice:3K-2:2025-09-01:4) confirms 'Added birth to month' in Section 3.3b, so this is supported. The answer also correctly cites 42 CFR 431.51(a)(1) which appears in the evidence. Citation quality is high with specific section references (3K-2 § 3.3, § 5.4.5, § 6.5, etc.). A Medicaid policy expert would find this answer thorough and well-organized.

Medicaid shall cover procedures, products, and services related to this policy when they are medically necessary, and:
the procedure, product, or service is individualized, specific, and consistent with symptoms or confirmed diagnosis of the illness or injury under treatment, and not in excess of the beneficiary's needs;
the procedure, product, or service can be safely furnished, and no equally effective and more conservative or less costly treatment is available statewide; and
the procedure, product, or service is furnished in a manner not primarily intended for the convenience of the beneficiary, the beneficiary's caretaker, or the provider.

ID: sec:doc:clinical_policy:3K-2:3.3
Title: 3.3 Transfers of Eligible Beneficiaries
Section: 3.3
Policy: 3K-2
Type: clinical_policy
Effective: 2025-09-01
Citation link: [Community Alternatives Program for Disabled Adults (CAP/DA)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment)

Content:
When a transfer request is received, by the Case Management Entity (CME), the CME shall coordinate the transfer of an eligible CAP/DA beneficiary to another county or entity within the approved, agreed upon transition date or less than 30 calendar days of the request to transfer.
CME shall coordinate the transfer to prevent gaps in service provisions. The following steps must be completed prior to the transfer:
determine anticipated start date of service;
coordinate transition plan between provider agencies;
discuss and plan for the health, safety and well-being of the beneficiary;
initiate in the CAP Business System (e-CAP/DA) the transfer of the electronic health records to the receiving county;
arrange for a home visit within five (5) business days of the date the CAP/DA beneficiary moves to their new primary residence by the receiving entity to assess the home environment identifying any health and welfare concerns and planning for mitigation and safety; and
coordinate and plan the provision of services to start on the first date of the transfer.
For a CAP/C beneficiary aging out of CAP/C and wishes to transfer to CAP/DA:
The CAP/C CME designee shall implement a transition, transfer plan 12 months prior to the birth month. These coordination activities are:
Completion of a transition plan during the annual needs review assessment that occurs at age 20; and
Consultation with the CAP/C beneficiary and primary caregiver to educate about other Medicaid and community resources to meet needs after the age of 21.
Three months (90 calendar days) prior to the birth month or identified transfer month, a multidisciplinary team meeting must be convened to discuss care needs and to ensure the identified formal and informal resources are able to meet care needs.
The month prior to the birth month, the local DSS must be notified of the need to change the CAP evidence code for CAP/DA participation for the identified CAP/DA effective start date.
On the first day of the birth month or identified transfer month, CAP/DA services are authorized and provided to the beneficiary.
Note: A Service Request Form (SFR) is not required. An assessment is required to identify ongoing adult needs for the generation of an adult service plan.
For a CAP/DA beneficiary transferring to a different county:
The CME designee of the transferring agency shall coordinate the transfer with the CME designee of the receiving agency upon the agreed upon transfer date or less than 30 calendar days of the request to transfer.
The CME designee of the transferring and receiving agencies shall discuss and plan for the health, safety and well-being of the beneficiary.
The electronic health record is transferred to the receiving county.
The CME designee of the receiving agency shall arrange for a home visit within five (5) business days of the date the CAP/DA beneficiary moves in their new primary residence to assess the environment to identify any health and welfare concerns to plan for mitigation and safety.
The CME designee shall coordinate and plan the provision of services to start on the first date of the transfer into the receiving county.
Note: An active beneficiary previously approved to participate in CAP/DA can continue to participate in the program when a transfer to another county occurs. A transferring beneficiary continues to be eligible for CAP/DA regardless of their county of residence.  Ongoing Medicaid eligibility is determined at the next Medicaid certification period.
When a waitlist is active in the transferring county, the CAP/DA beneficiary is considered in a priority category and guaranteed a slot immediately in the receiving county.

register as a user of the CAP Business System (e-CAP) and participate in required trainings.

ID: sec:doc:clinical_policy:3K-2:5.4.5
Title: 5.4.5 Changes and Revision to the Service Plan
Section: 5.4.5
Policy: 3K-2
Type: clinical_policy
Effective: 2025-09-01
Citation link: [Community Alternatives Program for Disabled Adults (CAP/DA)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment)

Content:
A plan of care (POC) revision is required when a request is made to add, reduce, increase, delete a CAP/DA service or Medicaid State service, or when there are changes in a service provider. The Case Management Entity (CME) designee is responsible for revising the POC when there is a change in the beneficiary's needs.
Service plan revisions are approved by unbiased personnel within the CME. Revisions for an urgent need because of a critical change in status may be approved retroactively for up to 30 calendar days prior to the date that the plan is revised. The beneficiary or the primary caregiver shall agree to and sign and date the service plan acknowledging changes for CAP/DA provisions.
Note : Specified plan of care revisions may require a minor change to the approval without the legal guardian or the primary caregiver's signature. The eCAP Business System provides guidance in that area.
Service plan revisions, excluding goods and services, training, education, and consultative services, home and vehicle modifications and assistive technology, may be approved retroactively for up to 30 calendar days, when an urgent need is identified that places the CAP/DA beneficiary at risk of losing their community placement. The service, equipment or supply cannot be procured prior to the first day of the 30-calendar day retroactive date. The beneficiary or the primary caregiver shall agree to and sign and date the service plan acknowledging changes for CAP/DA provision.
Note: The items listed above as exclusion for retroactive approval, may be considered for urgent approval based on necessary need. The POC must be submitted into the CAP Business System along with supporting documentation.

ID: sec:doc:federal_regulation:42-CFR-431:431.51
Title: Free choice of providers
Section: 431.51
Policy: 42-CFR-431
Type: federal_regulation
Last revised: 2007-12-04
Federal Register cite: [56 FR 8847, Mar. 1, 1991, as amended at 67 FR 41094, June 14, 2002; 72 FR 68091, Dec. 4, 2007]
Citation link: [42 CFR Part 431](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-431)

Content:
(a) Statutory basis. This section is based on sections 1902(a)(23), 1902(e)(2), and 1915(a) and (b) and 1932(a)(3) of the Act.

(1) Section 1902(a)(23) of the Act provides that beneficiaries may obtain services from any qualified Medicaid provider that undertakes to provide the services to them.

(2) Section 1915(a) of the Act provides that a State shall not be found out of compliance with section 1902(a)(23) solely because it imposes certain specified allowable restrictions on freedom of choice.

(3) Section 1915(b) of the Act authorizes waiver of the section 1902(a)(23) freedom of choice of providers requirement in certain specified circumstances, but not with respect to providers of family planning services.

(4) Section 1902(a)(23) of the Act provides that a beneficiary enrolled in a primary care case management system or Medicaid managed care organization (MCO) may not be denied freedom of choice of qualified providers of family planning services.

(5) Section 1902(e)(2) of the Act provides that an enrollee who, while completing a minimum enrollment period, is deemed eligible only for services furnished by or through the MCO or PCCM, may, as an exception to the deemed limitation, seek family planning services from any qualified provider.

(6) Section 1932(a) of the Act permits a State to restrict the freedom of choice required by section 1902(a)(23), under specified circumstances, for all services except family planning services.

(b) State plan requirements. A State plan, except the plan for Puerto Rico, the Virgin Islands, or Guam, must provide as follows:

(1) Except as provided under paragraph (c) of this section and part 438 of this chapter, a beneficiary may obtain Medicaid services from any institution, agency, pharmacy, person, or organization that is—

(i) Qualified to furnish the services; and

(ii) Willing to furnish them to that particular beneficiary.

This includes an organization that furnishes, or arranges for the furnishing of, Medicaid services on a prepayment basis.

(2) A beneficiary enrolled in a primary care case-management system, a Medicaid MCO, or other similar entity will not be restricted in freedom of choice of providers of family planning services.

(c) Exceptions. Paragraph (b) of this section does not prohibit the agency from—

(1) Establishing the fees it will pay providers for Medicaid services;

(2) Setting reasonable standards relating to the qualifications of providers; or

(3) Subject to paragraph (b)(2) of this section, restricting beneficiaries' free choice of providers in accordance with one or more of the exceptions set forth in § 431.54, or under a waiver as provided in § 431.55; or

(4) Limiting the providers who are available to furnish targeted case management services defined in § 440.169 of this chapter to target groups that consist solely of individuals with developmental disabilities or with chronic mental illness. This limitation may only be permitted so that the providers of case management services for eligible individuals with developmental disabilities or with chronic mental illness are capable of ensuring that those individuals receive needed services.

(d) Certification requirement —(1) Content of certification. If a State implements a project under one of the exceptions allowed under § 431.54 (d), (e) or (f), it must certify to CMS that the statutory safeguards and requirements for an exception under section 1915(a) of the Act are met.

(2) Timing of certification. (i) For an exception under § 431.54(d), the State may not institute the project until after it has submitted the certification and CMS has made the findings required under the Act, and so notified the State.

(ii) For exceptions under § 431.54 (e) or (f), the State must submit the certificate by the end of the quarter in which it implements the project.

per_question.question: Is there a maximum earned income limit for people on HCWD (Health Coverage for Workers with Disabilities), and what premiums apply?
per_question.agent_answer:
## Income limit

[unverified: There is no maximum earned-income limit for HCWD.] HCWD eligibility instead bars a person whose unearned income exceeds 150% of the federal poverty level (FPL); [unverified: countable income above that level affects cost-sharing.] Eligibility also requires, among other things, employment, disability under the applicable standard, and meeting the HCWD income requirements.

NC Medicaid determines countable income after applicable exclusions, including work-expense exclusions for blind people and impairment-related work-expense exclusions for disabled people.

## Fees and monthly premiums

- At or below 150% FPL: no HCWD cost-sharing other than applicable copayments.
- Above 150% FPL: a $50 enrollment fee is due for each 12-month certification period.
- Above 200% FPL: the person pays the $50 enrollment fee plus a monthly premium.
- Premiums rise by income band through 450% FPL; at 451% FPL and above, the monthly premium is $875 for either an individual or couple.

| Countable-income band | Individual monthly premium | Couple monthly premium |
|---|---:|---:|
| 0–150% FPL | $0 | $0 |
| 151–200% FPL | $0 | $0 |
| 201–250% FPL | $196 | $265 |
| 251–300% FPL | $235 | $318 |
| 301–350% FPL | $274 | $370 |
| 351–400% FPL | $313 | $423 |
| 401–450% FPL | $352 | $476 |
| 451% FPL and above | $875 | $875 |



Members of federally recognized Native American tribes and Alaska Natives are exempt from HCWD cost-sharing, including both enrollment fees and premiums.

The current chart was updated for 2026 and became effective April 1, 2026.

---

- [MA-2180 § F. Income](https://policies.ncdhhs.gov/wp-content/uploads/MA-2180-HCWD-ADA-Approval.pdf)
- [MA-2180 § A. Generally](https://policies.ncdhhs.gov/wp-content/uploads/MA-2180-HCWD-ADA-Approval.pdf)
- [MA-2180 § A. Enrollment Fee](https://policies.ncdhhs.gov/wp-content/uploads/MA-2180-HCWD-ADA-Approval.pdf)
- [MA-2180 § B. Premiums](https://policies.ncdhhs.gov/wp-content/uploads/MA-2180-HCWD-ADA-Approval.pdf)
- [CHANGE NOTICE FOR MANUAL NO. 05-26 § IV. EFFECTIVE DATE AND IMPLEMENTATION](https://policies.ncdhhs.gov/wp-content/uploads/CN_05-26.docx.pdf)

| 201–250% FPL | $196 | $265 |
| 251–300% FPL | $235 | $318 |
| 301–350% FPL | $274 | $370 |
| 351–400% FPL | $313 | $423 |
| 401–450% FPL | $352 | $476 |
| 451% FPL and above | $875 | $875 |



Members of federally recognized Native American tribes and Alaska Natives are exempt from HCWD cost-sharing, including both enrollment fees and premiums.

Calculate the amount of total countable net earned and unearned income for the individual.

per_question.question: What is the federal statutory authority for NC's CAP/DA waiver, and what does the state need to demonstrate in its waiver application?
per_question.agent_answer:
## Federal statutory authority

NC’s CAP/DA program is a **Medicaid home- and community-based services (HCBS) waiver under Social Security Act § 1915(c)**. That provision authorizes the Secretary to permit Medicaid payment for approved HCBS—other than room and board—under a written plan of care for people who, without those services, would require hospital, nursing-facility, or ICF/IID-level care. [Social Security Act — Title XIX (Medicaid)](https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-prelim-title42-chapter7-subchapter19)

The statute permits a § 1915(c) waiver to waive the ordinary Medicaid requirements of **statewideness, comparability, and certain community income/resource rules**. [Social Security Act — Title XIX (Medicaid)](https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-prelim-title42-chapter7-subchapter19)

## What North Carolina must show in its waiver application

Under the governing federal application regulation, the State must submit the assurances required by 42 CFR § 441.302 and documentation required by § 441.303; where applicable, it must also request the particular statutory waivers it needs and state whether it will decline HCBS when expected waiver costs exceed the cost of equivalent institutional care. [42 CFR Part 441](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-441)

The application must show that waiver services will be provided through a Medicaid-agency-approved, written person-centered service plan; only to people who are not institutional inpatients; and only to people whom the State determines would need the applicable Medicaid-covered institutional level of care without HCBS. [42 CFR Part 441](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-441)

It must also identify the qualifications of the people who develop plans of care, define the target population, and separately define each waiver service rather than using open-ended or improperly consolidated service descriptions. [42 CFR Part 441](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-441)

### Required assurances and supporting proof

The State must provide satisfactory assurances of:

- **Health and welfare safeguards**, including adequate provider standards, compliance with applicable licensure/certification requirements, HCBS-setting compliance, and an incident-management system. [42 CFR Part 441](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-441)  
- **Financial accountability**, including records supporting it and an independent audit of the waiver program. [42 CFR Part 441](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-441)  
- **Evaluation and periodic reevaluation** of participants’ institutional level-of-care need, with written documentation, identified evaluators and methods, and a reliable and comparable evaluation instrument where a different form is used. [42 CFR Part 441](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-441)  
- **Informed choice**: eligible people must be told of feasible waiver alternatives and allowed to choose institutional services or HCBS. [42 CFR Part 441](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-441)  
- **Cost neutrality**: the projected annual average per-capita cost of waiver and other Medicaid services for participants cannot exceed the estimated annual average per-capita cost absent the waiver. [Social Security Act — Title XIX (Medicaid)](https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-prelim-title42-chapter7-subchapter19) [42 CFR Part 441](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-441)  
- The number of unduplicated people the State intends to serve each year; that number becomes the waiver’s enrollment limit unless CMS approves an amendment increasing it. [42 CFR Part 441](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-441)  

The statutory assurance package also requires annual information to the Secretary about the waiver’s effect on the type and amount of Medicaid assistance and on recipients’ health and welfare. [Social Security Act — Title XIX (Medicaid)](https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-prelim-title42-chapter7-subchapter19)

## NC implementation and recent history

NC’s current CAP/DA clinical policy lists services including adult day health, in-home aide services, equipment/modifications/technology, meals, respite, personal emergency response services, medical supplies, case management, personal assistance, and financial management. [Community Alternatives Program for Disabled Adults (CAP/DA)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment)

CMS approved CAP/DA’s renewal effective November 1, 2024; NC’s Policy 3K-2 was revised effective September 1, 2025 to align with that renewal. [Policy 3K-2 Revision — 2025-09-01 (All sections and attachments)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment)

For regulatory history, the principal application rule, 42 CFR § 441.301, was last revised May 10, 2024, **89 FR 40863**. [42 CFR Part 441](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-441)

The answer goes into considerable detail about the specific regulatory requirements from 42 CFR 441.301 that align with the evidence provided.
